answer:
HYPOTHESIS (natural-language answer to "Is the relation between socioeconomic status and chances of degree completion affected by racial lines of the individual?"):

Socioeconomic status is positively associated with BA completion by the observation date in this NLS sample (pooled OR ≈ 1.34 per SES unit, 95% CI 1.07–1.67, p = 0.010; average marginal effect of +1 SD SES ≈ +0.44 percentage points on a 2.7% base rate). However, after adjusting for sex, family size, ASVAB ability, and class percentile, we find NO statistically detectable moderation of this SES–completion relation by race: the joint 2-df test of the SES×race interaction gives χ²(2) = 1.75, p = 0.42 (Wald p = 0.40), and the interaction fails to reach significance for either Black (SES×Black = +0.37, p = 0.18) or Hispanic (SES×Hispanic = +0.02, p = 0.96) respondents versus Whites. The point estimates hint at a steeper SES gradient for Black respondents (SES OR 1.82 per unit, 95% CI 1.11–3.00) than for White (1.26, 0.99–1.62) or Hispanic (1.28, 0.70–2.36) respondents — the opposite of the naive expectation that SES matters less for minorities — and this same ordering persists in every sensitivity analysis (Firth penalized logistic, within-race standardized SES, probability-scale contrasts), but the interaction test itself does not support a moderation conclusion. Given only 47 BA events among all non-White respondents, the correct phrasing is: no detectable moderation — not evidence of no moderation. What IS clearly moderated is the baseline level, not the gradient: White respondents complete BA at ~2.5–2.7× the rate of Black/Hispanic respondents (3.5% vs 1.3–1.4% unadjusted; race main effects remain positive for Black/Hispanic after SES adjustment, reflecting their lower SES levels).

=== SUPPORTING MODEL TABLE (main logistic GLM; White = reference; ability/1000, percentile/10) ===

race_Hisp   +0.268   0.261   +1.03  0.304  [-0.243, 0.780]   1.31
MALE        -0.268   0.144   -1.86  0.063

SES×Hisp    +0.015   0.325   +0.05  0.963

Race-specific SES effects (simple slopes + delta-method CIs):
  White:    β = +0.235 (SE 0.126)  OR/unit 1.26 [0.99–1.62]  OR/1 SD 1.19
  Black:    β = +0.601 (SE 0.254)  OR/unit 1.82 [1.11–3.00]  OR/1 SD 1.56
  Hispanic: β = +0.250 (SE 0.310)  OR/unit 1.28 [0.70–2.36]  OR/1 SD 1.20

Pooled/marginal SES effect (requested addition): model without interactions → SES OR 1.34 per unit [1.07–1.67], p = 0.0097; AME of +1 SD SES = +0.44 pp (mean predicted P(BA) 2.69% → 3.13%). The interaction test therefore FAILS TO SUPPORT race moderation of the SES gradient, while the pooled positive SES effect and the race gap in completion levels are both clearly supported.

Predicted P(BA), covariates at sample means (SES −2 → +2.2):
  White:    0.37% → 0.97%   (≈2.6× across SES range)
  Black:    0.27% → 3.31%   (≈12× across SES range)
  Hispanic: 0.46% → 1.31%   (≈2.8× across SES range)
(Black's steeper curve is visible but CIs overlap; at low SES minority probabilities are lowest.)

=== SENSITIVITY CHECKS ===
1. Firth penalized logistic (rare events, n=236 events): nearly identical — SES×Black +0.373 (z=1.38), SES×Hispanic +0.017 (z=0.05); race slopes White 1.27 [0.99–1.62], Black 1.84 [1.13–3.00], Hispanic 1.29 [0.71–2.33]. No convergence problems; no separation reversal.
2. SES standardized within race (handles differing within-race SDs 0.61–0.79): interaction LRT χ²(2)=1.32, p=0.52; slopes OR per within-race SD: White 1.18 [0.99–1.41], Black 1.44 [1.06–1.96], Hispanic 1.22 [0.75–1.97]. Same ordering, same null interaction.
3. Probability-scale view: mean ΔP(BA) for +1 SD SES: White +0.42 pp, Black +0.62 pp, Hispanic +0.51 pp — same modest ordering, far too small to distinguish groups at this base rate.
4. Unadjusted model (for contrast): SES×White interaction was significant (−0.76, p=0.003) with a steeper raw gradient for Black/Hispanic; the association attenuates to noise once ability, class percentile, and family size are controlled — i.e., the apparent raw moderation is largely absorbed by academic-ability and family-size differences.

=== INTERPRETIVE CAVEATS (carried in per your instruction) ===
(a) BA completion is measured as of the observation date; with only 2.7% completed, "not yet completed" ≠ "never completes" — the hypothesis concerns completion by the observed time, not lifetime attainment.
(b) The ABILITY composite is documented as a sum of ASVAB Z-scores, but observed values (1,016–3,068) are inconsistent with that description; it was treated as a continuous control. PERCENTILE IN CLASS direction is assumed higher-is-better (undocumented convention); its positive coefficient is consistent with that assumption.
(c) Because of event scarcity (28 Black, 19 Hispanic events), any null is phrased as "no detectable moderation," never proof of equality.
Also: cohort/year, SES composition, and weighting scheme are undocumented; analysis is unweighted, rows treated as independent (CASE IDs unique, no duplicates), no missing values, and no negative coded-missing values (SES negatives are legitimate values of an approximately standardized variable).

Artifacts: analysis_full.py (executed, full workflow), analysis_full_output.txt (complete output), inspection_first_look.py / inspection_output.txt (first-look stage).

payload.hypothesis: SES is positively associated with BA completion by the observation date (pooled OR 1.34/unit, 95% CI 1.07-1.67, p=0.010; +1 SD SES = +0.44 pp on a 2.7% base rate), but after adjustment for sex, family size, ASVAB ability and class percentile, the joint 2-df SES x race interaction test is not significant (chi2(2)=1.75, p=0.42), so the data provide no detectable evidence that the SES-completion gradient is moderated by race. Point estimates consistently hint at a steeper SES gradient for Black respondents (OR 1.82 [1.11-3.00] per SES unit vs 1.26 [0.99-1.62] for White, 1.28 [0.70-2.36] for Hispanic), an ordering that persists across Firth penalized, within-race-standardized, and probability-scale sensitivity analyses, but never reaches interaction significance. Given only 47 BA events among non-White respondents this is 'no detectable moderation', not proof of no moderation. What is clearly differentiated by race is the baseline completion level (White 3.5% vs Black 1.3% / Hispanic 1.4%), not the SES gradient.
payload.workflow: Logistic GLM of BA DEGREE COMPLETED on SES x SAMPLE_RACE + sex + family size + ASVAB ability + class percentile (n=8,773; 236 events); joint 2-df LRT and Wald test of interactions; race-specific simple slopes with delta-method 95% CIs; pooled no-interaction model for the marginal SES effect; predicted-probability grid; Firth penalized logistic sensitivity; within-race standardized SES sensitivity; probability-scale (AME) view. Data: 8,773 rows, 0 missing, no coded-missing values; unweighted; White reference category.
